On 07/01/2026, a 15-year-old male with no documented past medical history, medications, or allergies presented to A&E with 3 days of worsening constant dull lower abdominal pain, constipation, reduced appetite, and mild nausea without vomiting, fever, urinary symptoms, or gastrointestinal bleeding. He was mildly dehydrated, with mild abdominal distension, lower abdominal tenderness, and mildly hypoactive or normal bowel sounds, but no guarding, rebound, peritonism, or haemodynamic instability. Pain improved from 6–7/10 to approximately 5/10 after IV fluids.

Abdominal X-ray demonstrated significant faecal loading without obstruction or perforation. FBC, U&Es, CRP, and LFTs were normal. He received IV 0.9% sodium chloride 500 mL over 4 hours, was initially kept NBM/NPO, and was given a single oral dose of bisacodyl 10 mg. Paediatrics admitted him for supportive management and observation, with oral macrogol/Movicol, encouragement of oral fluids, and monitoring of bowel movements. Physiotherapy supported gentle mobilisation, and nursing and dietetic staff provided advice on hydration, fibre intake, and regular movement.

By 08/01/2026, he had passed a partial bowel movement with reduced pain and distension. Following a full bowel movement overnight, his abdominal pain resolved; he was clinically well with stable observations and a soft, non-tender abdomen without guarding or rebound. Oral macrogol was stopped, and lactulose 10 mL twice daily as required was prescribed for maintenance. He was discharged home with advice regarding a high-fibre diet, adequate oral hydration, and gentle walking. His GP was informed of the admission, discharge, and follow-up advice.

67-year-old man with hypertension and osteoarthritis, no regular medications or known drug allergies, presented on 01/01/2026 after a minor fall at home the previous evening and acute confusion. He had no loss of consciousness or focal neurological symptoms. Initial GCS was 12/15 with disorientation to time and place; blood pressure was 170/95 mmHg. CT head demonstrated a subdural hygroma without midline shift or acute haemorrhage. FBC, renal/electrolyte and coagulation studies were initially normal. He was admitted to the Neurology Ward for neurological observations and repeat imaging.

During admission, confusion gradually improved but persisted mildly for several days. Mild hyponatraemia (sodium 132 mmol/L) was identified and treated with oral sodium chloride 1 g three times daily with slow correction. Paracetamol 1 g four times daily was planned for mild headache. Neurological examinations remained stable, with no focal deficits, raised intracranial pressure, or meningism. Repeat CT head on 03/01/2026 showed no progression of the hygroma or new findings, and management was unchanged.

Physiotherapy and occupational therapy documented mild gait instability and impaired fine motor coordination affecting tasks such as fastening buttons and handling utensils. Mobility improved with supervised exercises, walking-frame use, balance training, and stair practice. Speech and language assessment showed adequate swallowing and communication, with mild word-finding difficulty attributed to residual confusion; no further intervention was required. OT provided home-safety education and recommended a raised toilet seat, bathroom and stair handrails, removal of loose rugs, improved lighting, and use of a grabber tool. Social and community support services were arranged for discharge planning.

By the later ward reviews, the patient was alert, increasingly oriented, and free of new neurological symptoms. Final physiotherapy assessments showed GCS 15/15, resolved confusion, independent walking over 15 metres, safe obstacle navigation, and ability to climb five steps using a handrail. He was considered fit for discharge home with support services and ongoing fall-prevention advice.

Discharge planning was completed in early January 2026, with GP and family updated. Atorvastatin 40 mg daily for 7 days and levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily for 7 days were documented in the discharge plan. Neurology follow-up was arranged in approximately 2 weeks to 1 month, with community support and home assessment recommended.

0f438665-d430-4adb-8acc-c3beed9e4942.final_summary:
A 3-year-old boy with allergies to pollen and macrolides, and no documented past medical history or regular medications, presented to A&E on 06/01/26 with 24–48 hours of poor oral intake, refusal of fluids, fewer wet nappies, mild fever and lethargy. There was no vomiting, diarrhoea, respiratory distress, rash, seizures or other concerning symptoms. Initial observations were temperature 38.3°C, HR 120 bpm, RR 22–24/min and SpO₂ 98% on room air. He was alert and interactive but mildly lethargic, with dry mucous membranes and capillary refill of approximately 2 seconds, consistent with mild dehydration. Examination showed mild nasal congestion, clear chest and a soft, non-tender abdomen.

The ED impression was viral illness/viral URTI with reduced intake and mild dehydration. No initial investigations were performed. He received paracetamol suspension 120 mg/5 mL, 5 mL, and a 10 mL/kg oral normal saline bolus, which was tolerated. He was admitted to the Paediatric Assessment Unit for observation and supportive care, including oral rehydration solution in small frequent amounts and IV 0.9% sodium chloride with 5% dextrose at 75% maintenance. Antibiotics were not planned.

During admission he remained mildly lethargic with persistent poor feeding and nasal congestion but no vomiting, diarrhoea or respiratory compromise. VBG showed mild metabolic acidosis (pH 7.33, bicarbonate 17 mmol/L). Management included IV fluids, PRN paracetamol, encouragement of oral fluids and small frequent feeds, and saline nasal drops. Parents received education regarding oral rehydration, feeding, and signs of worsening dehydration.

Oral intake and hydration subsequently improved, with tolerance of fluids and mashed food, resolution of fever, moist mucous membranes and improved activity. IV fluids were reduced to 50% maintenance to encourage oral intake. ENT assessment found moderate nasal mucosal inflammation consistent with viral URTI, without purulent discharge or anatomical abnormality. Saline spray/nasal irrigation and steam inhalation twice daily were advised.

By discharge, he was afebrile, alert and playful, eating and drinking better, with no signs of dehydration or respiratory distress. Final observations included HR 100 bpm, BP 90/60 mmHg, RR 22/min, temperature 36.8°C and SpO₂ 98% on room air. He was discharged home with advice to continue oral fluids and small meals, saline nasal drops as needed, saline nasal irrigation and steam inhalation twice daily. No new medications were prescribed; paracetamol could be used PRN for fever or discomfort. Parents understood the instructions and were advised to contact GP Dr Liu Tao or seek medical attention if feeding or hydration worsened, wet nappies decreased, or lethargy increased.

Initial management included IV 0.9% sodium chloride, IV paracetamol, 4-hourly neurological observations, repeat U&Es, oral hydration, and neurology liaison. Occupational therapy noted mild difficulty with fine motor tasks such as fastening buttons; a button hook and verbal prompts were recommended. Ceftriaxone was documented as continuing on day 2 of 5.

- **04/01/2026 onward:** The patient became alert and oriented and reported feeling well, with only mild fatigue initially. Gait remained mildly unsteady but improved with therapy. Sodium remained mildly low at 132–133 mmol/L. Oral sodium chloride supplementation was started, with doses documented as 1 g three times daily and later 600 mg three times daily, alongside fluid management including restriction to 1.5 L/day and repeat sodium monitoring. Mild evening headaches were treated with PRN paracetamol. Physiotherapy progressed through strengthening, dynamic balance work, parallel-bar exercises, and rollator-assisted gait training. Mild cognitive difficulties involving memory, attention, planning, and word finding were documented. - **05–07/01/2026:** The patient reported no new symptoms and increasing confidence with mobility. Neurological examinations remained stable, with no weakness, sensory loss, or other focal deficits. He mobilised with a rollator or walking aid, initially requiring assistance but progressively improving. Physiotherapy documented improved gait symmetry, balance, posture, and mobility. Recommendations included a grabber/reacher, non-slip mats, adaptive cutlery, a button hook, and a shower chair. Community care visits and follow-up therapy were arranged.

- **08/01/2026:** The patient was clinically stable with no headache, dizziness, confusion, or new neurological symptoms. Sodium remained mildly low at approximately 132–133 mmol/L and had been managed with oral sodium supplementation and fluid restriction. He could independently complete transfers and navigate stairs using aids, with only mild residual unsteadiness. Physiotherapy deemed him safe for discharge and arranged outpatient follow-up. Occupational therapy provided home safety equipment, and daily community care team visits were confirmed. He was discharged/planned for discharge with fall-prevention advice, GP follow-up within 7 days, neurology follow-up in approximately 2 weeks, and community physiotherapy. Paracetamol was prescribed as needed for pain or mild headache, with dosing instructions documented as 500 mg 1–2 tablets every 4–6 hours as needed and elsewhere as 1 g four times daily. He was advised to seek medical attention for worsening headache or confusion and to avoid anticoagulants unless prescribed.

IV 0.9% sodium chloride 1 L over 8 hours, oral hydration, fluid-balance monitoring, and repeat electrolytes were advised. Paracetamol 1 g every 6 hours as required was used for headache. Oral electrolyte supplementation with Dioralyte was initially provided, followed by sodium chloride tablets 600 mg twice daily. IV fluids were subsequently reduced and stopped. Occupational, speech and language, and physiotherapy assessments identified mild short-term memory, attention, sequencing, and word-finding difficulties, with initially mild unsteadiness requiring a four-wheel walker and supervision. By 09–10/01/26, the patient reported resolution of headache, dizziness, and confusion, with only mild fatigue. Mobility improved to safe unaided walking and stair navigation without dizziness or instability.

Chest X-ray demonstrated pneumomediastinum and subcutaneous emphysema, with no pneumothorax. He was advised to avoid Valsalva manoeuvres, straining, and heavy lifting. Repeat imaging showed a stable pneumomediastinum without progression. - **05–06/01/26:** Symptoms improved to mild residual chest discomfort, then resolved. Respiratory observations remained stable, with clear breath sounds and no respiratory distress. - **Subsequent review:** He remained clinically stable without chest pain or shortness of breath. Chest X-ray showed stable pneumomediastinum without complications; vital signs remained normal and there was no subcutaneous crepitus or respiratory distress. Discharge planning began, with advice regarding recurrence symptoms and when to seek urgent medical attention. Respiratory outpatient follow-up was planned.
